name: Penetrating and Blunt Neck Trauma, Maxillofacial Fractures, and Airway Emergencies

reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd ed / Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma
clinicalPearls: Anatomical neck zones comprise Zone I (clavicle to cricoid), Zone II (cricoid to mandible angle), and Zone III (mandible angle to skull base)
Hard signs of penetrating neck injury (expanding hematoma, active arterial bleeding, shock, absent carotid pulse) mandate emergency surgical exploration
Selective non-operative management guided by high-resolution CT angiography is safe for hemodynamically stable patients in all neck zones
Blunt cerebrovascular injury (BCVI) is diagnosed with Denver screening criteria and managed primarily with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy
Surgical cricothyroidotomy represents the definitive rapid emergency surgical airway of choice in failed or impossible endotracheal intubation
reference.pathophysiology: Penetrating neck trauma breaching the platysma muscle poses immediate threats to the airway, major vascular conduits (carotid arteries, internal jugular veins), and aerodigestive structures (trachea, esophagus). Vascular injury leads to exsanguinating external hemorrhage, expanding hematoma compressing the trachea, or ischemic cerebral infarction. Esophageal laceration causes rapid extravasation of saliva into the deep fascial spaces, precipitating virulent descending necrotizing mediastinitis within 24 to 48 hours.
additionalDifferentials: Zone I penetrating injury with mediastinal hematoma versus isolated proximal subclavian artery laceration
Tracheobronchial rupture versus tension pneumothorax with massive subcutaneous emphysema
Le Fort II pyramidal maxillary fracture versus Le Fort III craniofacial disjunction with skull base CSF leak
Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in orbital blowout fracture versus traumatic third cranial nerve palsy
additionalInvestigations: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the neck and brain from aortic arch to vertex
Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy for suspected airway disruption
Gastrografin water-soluble esophagogram followed by thin barium swallow or flexible esophagoscopy
Facial bones helical CT with 3D reconstructed slices for maxillofacial architectural evaluation
